questions.question: In a 3-hop onion-routing circuit (guard -> middle -> exit), which relay connects to the destination server?
options: The guard relay (entry hop)
The middle relay (transit hop)
The exit relay (outbound hop)
No relay connects directly
questions.explanation: The exit relay is the hop that makes the outbound connection to the destination.

questions.question: What does onion routing provide by itself for the payload contents between exit and destination?
options: No confidentiality unless an app-layer protocol provides it
End-to-end encryption for all traffic automatically
Perfect secrecy even against the destination server
A signature that authenticates the destination server
questions.explanation: Onion routing is about routing metadata; you still need HTTPS/TLS or similar to protect contents on the exit-to-destination leg.

questions.question: After a relay decrypts exactly one onion layer, what should it learn in the basic model?
options: The next hop and the remaining onion bytes
The client identity and the destination
The plaintext application message immediately
The full list of relays in the circuit
questions.explanation: Each hop peels one layer to learn only where to forward next and what bytes to forward.

questions.question: Why does the lesson's toy onion layer include an authentication tag (MAC) in addition to encryption?
options: To stop undetected edits to next-hop and inner bytes
To make ciphertext look random on the wire to observers
To let relays recover keys from packets later
To ensure repeated plaintext yields repeated ciphertext
questions.explanation: Without integrity, an attacker can flip bits to change routing metadata or create oracles via error behavior.

questions.question: What is a catastrophic failure mode for stream-cipher-like encryption if a (key, nonce) pair is reused?
options: XOR of ciphertexts reveals XOR of plaintexts
MAC verification becomes faster on average
Ciphertexts become smaller than plaintexts
Decryption works even with the wrong key
questions.explanation: Reusing a keystream lets an attacker combine ciphertexts to cancel the keystream and learn relationships between plaintexts.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes routing privacy from content privacy in onion routing?
options: Onion layers hide per-hop routing; HTTPS/TLS hides content
Onion layers alone hide content end-to-end without HTTPS/TLS
HTTPS/TLS alone hides routing path from relays without onion layers
Routing privacy and content privacy are the same thing
questions.explanation: Onion layers aim to limit what each relay learns about the route; content confidentiality still depends on the application-layer protocol.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what can a global passive adversary often do even if onion-layer cryptography is correct?
options: Correlate sender and receiver using timing/volume patterns
Break HMAC-SHA256 and decrypt all layers immediately
Compute private keys from public keys by brute force
Force relays to reveal the full circuit on demand
questions.explanation: Traffic analysis can correlate flows across hops without breaking the cryptography, especially without padding/batching defenses.

questions.question: In the toy implementation, what purpose does binding a layer to hop-specific AAD serve?
options: It stops cut-and-paste of a layer across hops or circuits
It makes encryption deterministic so packets can be cached
It lets relays skip tag verification for performance
It lets the exit decrypt all layers with one key
questions.explanation: AAD binds ciphertext to context; changing the hop name (or circuit metadata) causes tag verification to fail.
